text:
simon-customer: Hey team — after we upgraded k8s, several redwood-agent pods in namespace `redwood-agent` can't register with the private control plane. Agent logs show TLS handshake / DNS failures. Pastes below.

maria-support: Ok — can you share `kubectl get pods -n redwood-agent` and the failing pod log snippet? Also which control plane host/IP are the agents configured to reach? :mag_right:

simon-customer: Pods look mostly fine but one is CrashLoopBackOff:
```
$ kubectl get pods -n redwood-agent
NAME                                 READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
redwood-agent-7x9kq                  0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6          14m
redwood-agent-w4p2d                  1/1     Running            0          2d
```
Failing agent log:
```
2026-03-16T13:02:10Z INF connecting to control-plane private-control.example.corp:443
2026-03-16T13:02:10Z ERR tls handshake failed: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
2026-03-16T13:02:10Z ERR failing to register: tls: handshake failure
```
Agents are pointed at `private-control.example.corp` (internal VIP).

nina-se: Two quick checks: 1) Can the pod resolve that FQDN reliably? 2) Are there any NetworkPolicies or cluster egress allowlists blocking outbound to the VIP? Run from the agent namespace:
```
kubectl run -it --rm debug-shell --image=radial/busyboxplus:curl -n redwood-agent -- sh
# inside
nslookup private-control.example.corp
curl -v https://private-control.example.corp:443
```

simon-customer: Ran the commands. nslookup sometimes times out, curl connects then resets:
```
$ nslookup private-control.example.corp
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
$ curl -v https://private-control.example.corp:443
*   Trying 10.12.34.56:443...
* TCP_NODELAY set
* Connected to private-control.example.corp (10.12.34.56) port 443 (#0)
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
* server certificate verification OK
* Closing connection 0
curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
```
We also have namespaces with default-deny egress and a perimeter firewall that only allows some outbound CIDRs.

aj-platform: That pattern suggests either intermittent DNS, a network policy/egress ACL dropping packets mid-handshake (often due to TLS proxy), or the control-plane IP not in the firewall allowlist. Could also be SNI-based interception.

maria-support: Please `kubectl describe networkpolicy -A` and show any deny policies that could affect agent traffic. Also check node-level iptables/firewall and the perimeter egress ACL for the control-plane IP/CIDR and port 443.

simon-customer: Posted netpol outputs:
```
$ kubectl get networkpolicy -A
NAMESPACE           NAME                    POD-SELECTOR   AGE
customer-apps       default-deny-egress     app=web        6d
redwood-agent       (none)

$ kubectl describe networkpolicy default-deny-egress -n customer-apps
PodSelector: app=web
PolicyTypes: Egress
Egress:
  to:
  - ipBlock: 10.0.0.0/8
  ports: 80, 443
```
Note: default-deny only in `customer-apps`. CNI is weave-net. We also have a cluster-wide perimeter firewall that filters outbound IPs.

nina-se: Namespaced netpols shouldn't block `redwood-agent` namespace unless there are cross-namespace selectors. But the perimeter firewall or any transparent TLS inspection could still be the root cause. Do node-level tests too:

maria-support: From a node run:
```
dig +short private-control.example.corp
curl -v --resolve private-control.example.corp:443:10.12.34.56 https://private-control.example.corp:443
openssl s_client -connect 10.12.34.56:443 -servername private-control.example.corp
```
Look for substituted certs / proxy CA.

Also try a temporary permissive NetworkPolicy in `redwood-agent` to isolate k8s netpol vs external firewall:
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-all-egress-temp
  namespace: redwood-agent
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - {}
```
If registration succeeds, it's a netpol issue. If not, likely external firewall/TLS proxy.

simon-customer: We ran node tests and found a transparent TLS inspection proxy on the path that replaces server certs with the proxy's cert (internal CA). `openssl s_client` returned the proxy cert chain. Also the perimeter ACL was intermittently blocking the control-plane VIP. So two issues: TLS interception and an egress ACL missing the control-plane IP.

maria-support: OK — remediation options:
- If TLS interception is required, add the inspection CA to the agent container's system trust store (mount as a secret/configmap and place in /etc/ssl/certs or update ca-certificates). Restart agents.
- Prefer not to intercept TLS for control-plane traffic: whitelist the control-plane FQDN/IP on the perimeter appliance and allow direct 443 without interception.

Sample narrow NetworkPolicy to explicitly allow only control-plane IP on 443 from agents (replace CIDR):
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-controlplane-egress
  namespace: redwood-agent
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.12.34.56/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
```

nina-se: Agents rely on the container image's CA store. If you inject the proxy CA, ensure it's available before the agent starts (or use an initContainer) and then recreate pods.

aj-platform: Escalating to eng-infra (INC-2026-451) to track docs and recommended firewall/CNI guidance for weave-net + enterprise inspection proxies.

simon-customer: Update — after adding the control-plane IP/CIDR to the perimeter allowlist and excluding the FQDN from TLS inspection, the failing agent pod registered successfully:
```
2026-03-16T13:35:21Z INF registered with control plane as agent-7x9kq
```
Thanks for the help!

maria-support: Great — we're marking this resolved in the thread. We'll keep INC-2026-451 open for follow-up docs and agent truststore UX improvements. :thumbsup:
